questiontext.text: How is a skew heap best described?

answer.text: A self-adjusting, amortized version of a leftist heap

feedback.text: Correct — it is the bookkeeping-free, amortized analog of a leftist heap.
No — that describes a binary heap, not a skew heap.
No — a skew heap maintains heap order, not search order.

answer.text: A heap with guaranteed O(1) worst-case merge

feedback.text: No — its O(log n) merge bound is amortized, not worst-case per operation.

generalfeedback.text: A skew heap is a self-adjusting mergeable heap: the amortized, no-bookkeeping counterpart of the leftist heap.

questiontext.text: During a skew-heap merge, after linking along the right paths, what does the algorithm do at each merged node?

answer.text: Unconditionally swaps its left and right children

feedback.text: Correct — the unconditional child swap is the self-adjusting heuristic.

answer.text: Swaps children only if the s-values violate the leftist property

feedback.text: No — that is the leftist heap; skew heaps swap unconditionally and track no s-values.

answer.text: Recolors the node red or black

feedback.text: No — that belongs to red-black trees.
No — no rotations or height checks are performed.

generalfeedback.text: As the merge descends the right paths, it unconditionally swaps the children of each node it visits — no condition, no stored balance data.

questiontext.text: What is the time bound for skew-heap merge/insert/extract-min?

feedback.text: Correct — the swap heuristic guarantees a logarithmic amortized bound.

answer.text: O(log n) worst-case per single operation

feedback.text: No — a single operation can be worse; the O(log n) bound is amortized.
No — merge-based operations are logarithmic, not constant.
No — that would defeat the purpose of the structure.

generalfeedback.text: Skew-heap operations are O(log n) amortized; individual operations may occasionally cost more, but the amortized bound holds.

questiontext.text: Compared to a leftist heap, a skew heap:

answer.text: Stores no s-value / balance information, making nodes simpler

feedback.text: Correct — it drops the null-path-length bookkeeping entirely.

answer.text: Requires an extra balance byte per node

feedback.text: No — it removes bookkeeping rather than adding it.

answer.text: Gives worst-case rather than amortized guarantees

feedback.text: No — it trades the leftist worst-case bound for an amortized one.
No — merge is precisely its core operation.

generalfeedback.text: A skew heap stores no s-values: it is simpler than a leftist heap and self-adjusts via unconditional swaps, at the cost of amortized (not worst-case) bounds.

questiontext.text: As in a leftist heap, insert and extract-min in a skew heap are implemented via merge.

feedback.text: Correct — insert merges a singleton; extract-min merges the root's two subtrees.
Both operations are built on merge, just as in a leftist heap.

questiontext.text: A skew heap swaps a node's children only when a stored s-value indicates the leftist property is violated.

feedback.text: No — that describes a leftist heap; a skew heap swaps unconditionally and stores no s-value.
Correct — skew heaps swap children unconditionally, with no s-value check.

questiontext.text: The self-adjusting action a skew heap performs on children at each visited node during merge is to ______ them.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct — a synonym for swap.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a skew heap are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is a self-adjusting mergeable heap with O(log n) amortized operations

feedback.text: Yes — that is its performance profile.

answer.text: Its merge unconditionally swaps children as it melds down the right paths

feedback.text: Yes — the unconditional swap is what makes it self-adjusting.

answer.text: It stores a null-path-length s-value in every node

feedback.text: No — it stores no such balance data; that is the leftist heap.

answer.text: It guarantees O(log n) worst-case per single operation

feedback.text: No — its bound is amortized, not per-operation worst-case.

generalfeedback.text: A skew heap is a self-adjusting mergeable heap: unconditional child swaps during merge, O(log n) amortized cost, and no stored s-values — simpler than a leftist heap.
